subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On the Tannenbaum-Schmidt continuum, moving from left to right shows:
options: Decreasing manager authority and increasing subordinate freedom
A shift from democratic to autocratic styles only
No change in the balance of authority
Increasing manager authority and decreasing subordinate freedom
questions.explain: The continuum runs from manager-led (boss-centred) to subordinate-led (freedom for staff) leadership.

questions.q: The Hawthorne effect, identified by Elton Mayo, suggests that productivity rises when:
options: Pay is linked directly to output
Workers feel they are receiving attention and are valued
Managers adopt a strictly autocratic style
Tasks are broken into the smallest possible parts
questions.explain: Mayo found output improved because workers felt observed and valued, highlighting social/human factors.

questions.q: If a product is price inelastic, a firm wishing to increase total revenue should:
options: Lower the price
Give the product away free
Raise the price, since quantity demanded falls less than proportionately
Keep the price fixed forever
questions.explain: For inelastic demand a price rise lowers quantity by a smaller proportion, so total revenue increases.

questions.q: Targeting the over-65s with stairlifts is an example of segmentation by:
options: Geographic factors
Demographic factors (age)
Behavioural factors
Psychographic factors only
questions.explain: Age is a demographic variable, so targeting by age range is demographic segmentation.

questions.q: A 'dog' in the Boston Matrix is best described as a product with:
options: Low market share in a low-growth market
Rapidly rising sales
High share in a growing market
High share in a high-growth market
questions.explain: Dogs have low share in low-growth markets and are often candidates for divestment.

questions.q: Which formula correctly gives the absenteeism rate?
options: Output ÷ number of staff present
(Number of staff days absent ÷ total possible working days) × 100
(Total wages ÷ number of staff) × 100
(Number of staff who left ÷ total staff) × 100
questions.explain: Absenteeism rate = (number of staff days lost to absence ÷ total possible working days) × 100.

questions.q: An autocratic leadership style is characterised by:
options: No decisions being made at all
Decisions made by the leader with little consultation
Decisions reached by group consensus
Decisions delegated entirely to employees
questions.explain: Autocratic leaders make decisions themselves and expect compliance, with little staff input.

questions.q: Taylor's theory of scientific management assumes that workers are primarily motivated by:
options: Money and economic reward
Recognition and responsibility
Self-actualisation
Social belonging and team relationships
questions.explain: Taylor argued workers are 'economic men' motivated chiefly by pay, leading to piece-rate systems.

questions.q: A piece-rate payment system pays workers according to:
options: The number of hours worked
Company profits shared equally
The number of units they produce
A fixed annual salary
questions.explain: Piece rate links pay directly to output, paying a set amount per unit produced.

questions.q: Setting a specific HR objective, such as reducing labour turnover to 10%, is most useful because it:
options: Provides a measurable target to plan towards and assess
Removes the need to measure performance
Replaces the need for any motivation strategy
Guarantees the objective will be met
questions.explain: A specific, measurable HR objective allows the firm to plan, monitor and evaluate performance.

questions.q: A penetration pricing strategy involves:
options: Matching exactly the prices of all competitors
Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly
Charging different prices to different segments
Setting a deliberately high initial price to skim early adopters
questions.explain: Penetration pricing uses a low launch price to win customers and build market share rapidly.

questions.q: Which is a key benefit of decentralisation?
options: It reduces the need to train junior staff
Senior managers retain tight control over all decisions
Local managers can respond quickly to local conditions
Decisions are made more consistently across the whole firm
questions.explain: Decentralisation pushes authority down so local managers can make faster, more responsive decisions.

questions.q: Product portfolio analysis is mainly used to:
options: Calculate a firm's tax bill
Assess the balance of a firm's range of products and guide investment decisions
Decide a single product's price only
Recruit marketing staff
questions.explain: Portfolio analysis, e.g. the Boston Matrix, reviews the mix of products to inform investment and marketing strategy.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Herzberg motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
options: Achievement and recognition
Company policy
Salary
Working conditions
questions.explain: Motivators such as achievement, recognition and responsibility drive satisfaction; the others are hygiene factors.

questions.q: Price skimming is most appropriate when:
options: The firm wants the lowest possible margin
A new, innovative product has few competitors and customers willing to pay a premium
Demand is perfectly elastic
A product is a generic commodity with many substitutes
questions.explain: Skimming sets a high initial price to exploit early adopters of an innovative product before competitors enter.

questions.q: Collective bargaining is the process by which:
options: Shareholders decide directors' pay
Each employee negotiates pay individually with the employer
Government sets wage rates for all firms
Trade unions negotiate pay and conditions on behalf of members
questions.explain: Collective bargaining is negotiation of terms between employers and unions representing groups of workers.

questions.q: Hard HRM treats employees primarily as:
options: A valued asset to be developed and empowered
A resource/cost to be used efficiently and flexibly
Equal partners in strategic decisions
Members of a single family unit
questions.explain: Hard HRM views workers as a resource to be deployed cost-effectively, in contrast to soft HRM.

questions.q: The marketing mix for a service business is most commonly extended from the 4 Ps to the 7 Ps by adding:
options: Place, Promotion and Packaging
People, Process and Physical evidence
Positioning, Profit and Process
Profit, Price and Promotion
questions.explain: The 7 Ps add People, Process and Physical evidence to the original Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

questions.q: An advantage of intuitive decision-making over scientific decision-making is that it:
options: Is always more accurate
Requires large research budgets
Eliminates all risk
Can be faster and useful where data is unavailable or markets change rapidly
questions.explain: Intuition allows quick decisions when reliable data is lacking or conditions move too fast for full research.

questions.q: Which is an example of a non-financial method of motivation?
options: Teamworking
Commission
Performance-related pay
Profit sharing
questions.explain: Teamworking is a non-financial method; the others are financial reward systems.

questions.q: Off-the-job training refers to training that takes place:
options: At the employee's normal workstation while working
Away from the immediate work area, e.g. on a course
Exclusively through job rotation
Only after the employee has resigned
questions.explain: Off-the-job training occurs away from the workplace, such as at college or on external courses.

questions.q: A laissez-faire leadership style is most likely to be effective when:
options: Tasks are highly routine and standardised
Staff are inexperienced and need close direction
A crisis requires fast top-down decisions
Staff are highly skilled, motivated and self-directing
questions.explain: Laissez-faire leaves staff to work autonomously, which suits skilled, self-motivated professionals.

questions.q: A USP (unique selling point) helps a business by:
options: Removing the need to set a price
Making demand perfectly elastic
Giving a clear point of differentiation that makes its product stand out from rivals
Increasing variable costs
questions.explain: A USP differentiates a product, helping it stand out and reducing direct price competition.

questions.q: A firm has 200 staff; 30 leave and are replaced during the year. Its labour turnover is:
questions.explain: Labour turnover = (staff leaving ÷ average number employed) × 100 = (30 ÷ 200) × 100 = 15%.

questions.q: A matrix organisational structure is best described as one where employees:
options: Work across functions, reporting to both a functional and a project manager
Have no formal hierarchy at all
Are grouped strictly by geographic region
Report only to a single line manager
questions.explain: In a matrix structure staff belong to a function but also work on projects, answering to two managers.

questions.q: The span of control refers to:
options: The degree of decision-making authority delegated
The number of layers in the hierarchy
The chain of command from top to bottom
The number of subordinates directly answerable to a manager
questions.explain: Span of control is the number of subordinates directly accountable to one manager.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which level must generally be satisfied before esteem needs?
options: Self-actualisation
Social (love/belonging) needs
Aesthetic needs
Self-fulfilment
questions.explain: Maslow's order is physiological, safety, social, esteem, then self-actualisation, so social needs precede esteem.

questions.q: The promotion element of the marketing mix is mainly concerned with:
options: Where the product is sold
Setting the unit cost
Communicating with customers to inform and persuade them to buy
Designing the product's function
questions.explain: Promotion covers advertising, PR and sales methods used to inform and persuade customers.

questions.q: Product positioning refers to:
options: The order in which products are launched
The stage of the product life cycle
How a product is perceived by consumers relative to competitors in their minds
The physical place a product occupies in a warehouse
questions.explain: Positioning concerns the image and perception a product holds in consumers' minds compared with rivals.

questions.q: Quantitative data differs from qualitative data in that quantitative data:
options: Cannot be put into charts
Explains consumers' opinions and motivations
Is numerical and can be measured and statistically analysed
Always comes from focus groups
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical and measurable, whereas qualitative data captures opinions and reasons.
